How Companies Find Employees Contractors rely on a mix of informal and formal strategies to find new employees, as shown in Figure 8. More than 50% of contractors reported that recommendations and online job boards are two of the top ways their company finds new workers. Figure 8. Approaches to finding new workers The prominence of personal networks underscores the importance of trust and reputation in the trades, whereas online boards and apprenticeships or internships suggest an openness to newcomers in the trades. These findings indicate that contractors value candidates who are vetted and have had some exposure to the industry, either through work experience (recommendations) 16 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. or through structured or on-the-job training (trade/vocational schools and apprenticeships or internships). Additionally, the variability in responses demonstrates that contractors use a mix of recruiting strategies, including leveraging online avenues such as job boards, company websites, and social media. Most Important Traits for a New Hire When asked to rank the most important traits for new hires from 1 (most important) to 10 (least important), respondents placed strong emphasis on technical skills, with 18% of respondents listing it as the most important trait. Arriving to work on time and ready to work was the top trait for 13%, and valuing a job done right was the top trait for 12%. Having union membership was the least important trait for 39% of respondents, which likely reflects the types of companies that responded, as a majority of residential building work is non-union. Most and least important traits for a new hire Hiring Versus Training Survey responses revealed distinct circumstances that influence contractors when deciding whether to train an existing worker or hire a new one. A summary of themes and their frequency between the two paths is shown in Table 4. Companies overwhelmingly prefer investing in training when the worker already has a solid foundation of skills and only needs minimal training to fill gaps. Training is also used when an existing worker fits well with organizational culture. Other reasons for training an existing worker include keeping up with new technologies or codes and investing in employee development to support retention and morale. In contrast, companies choose to hire new workers when workload growth or turnover creates capacity gaps, when the role requires a specialized or licensed skill set not available internally, 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. or when they need immediate expertise to keep up with project timelines. Hiring is often preferred when time is limited, the skill gap is too large to close through training, or when a new hire brings a fresh perspective or unique experience.
